questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Two centres sharing one region
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two centres can share one regional labour market
questions.stem: Two job centres share one metropolitan region; what best describes their labour market?

options.text: The two centres draw from one overlapping pool of workers across the region.
Each centre draws only from its own exclusive commuter zone without overlap.
options.misconception: assumes labour markets are sealed by distance

options.text: Workers never cross between the two centres territories in daily travel.
The larger centre absorbs all regional labour supply and leaves none.

questions.explanation: Shared regions produce overlapping commuter sheds; assuming sealed zones or single-centre dominance misreads the geography.

questions.topic: Suburbanisation and its fiscal cost

questions.stem: A workplace report shows per-capita infrastructure cost rising as density falls; what drives the rise?

options.text: Lower density spreads the same fixed cost over fewer taxpayers.
More road lane-kilometres must be maintained per resident.
Suburbs always generate higher property tax revenue per hectare.
Central cities have no infrastructure to maintain at all.

questions.explanation: Sprawl lengthens networks per resident, raising maintenance cost; revenue assumptions and ignoring legacy costs are wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Commuting shed and the transport that sustains it
questions.learningObjective: Explain what sustains a commuting shed
questions.stem: Explain why a radial rail line can sustain a long commuting shed from a city centre.

answer.exemplar: A radial rail line concentrates capacity along one corridor, lowering travel time and cost for distant workers, so the commuting shed stretches farther along that line than along roads.

questions.explanation: Radial rail lowers time and cost along a corridor, extending the shed; other modes or dispersed roads do not match this concentration.
questions.hint: Focus on capacity and travel time along one corridor.

A large park-and-ride lot replacing nearby housing.

A highway interchange with big-box retail around it.

questions.explanation: TOD mixes uses and walkability around transit; housing-only, parking, or highway retail miss the concept.

questions.stem: Centre land value is 500; it falls by 20 per kilometre; what is it 4 km out?
questions.explanation: 500 minus 20 times 4 equals 420; multiplying 500 by 0.2 would misstate the drop.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Urban heat island mechanism
questions.stem: Why is the urban heat island strongest at night?

options.text: Cities cool faster than rural areas at night.
Solar radiation peaks after dark.
Stored heat is released slowly after sunset.
Wind always stops at night in cities.

questions.explanation: Slow release of stored heat strengthens the island at night; solar peaks or faster cooling are wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Heat island magnitude between two sites
questions.stem: A report claims a 10-degree heat island; what should be checked first?

options.text: Whether the city has any trees at all.
Whether the instruments were painted black.
Whether the measurement was taken at noon only.
Whether the two sites differ in elevation or land cover.

questions.explanation: Elevation or land-cover differences can inflate magnitude; instrument paint or tree presence are not the first check.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Where a monitoring network is sited
questions.stem: A city has 5 monitors covering 100 square kilometres; what area does each monitor represent on average?
questions.explanation: 100 divided by 5 equals 20 square kilometres; multiplying 5 by 100 inverts it.
questions.hint: Divide total area by monitor count.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Siting bias in a monitoring network
questions.stem: A network has twice as many monitors in the north as the south; what follows?

options.text: The south has no pollution at all.
Northern conditions are better resolved than southern ones.
Monitor count has no effect on resolution.
The north must be more polluted.

questions.explanation: More monitors improve resolution in the north; denying pollution or count effects is wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A flood plain and the restriction it motivates
questions.stem: Explain why preserving open flood-plain land helps manage floods.

answer.exemplar: Open flood-plain land stores excess water during high flows, reducing downstream peak levels and protecting built areas.

questions.explanation: Open land stores excess water and lowers downstream peaks; omitting storage is incomplete.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Wetland and the protection it gives
questions.stem: A catchment is 800 square kilometres and wetlands cover 80; what share is wetland?
questions.explanation: 80 divided by 800 equals 0.1; using 800 over 80 inverts the share.
questions.hint: Divide wetland area by catchment area.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Compact footprint as a share of the sprawled one

stimulus.body: A workplace report compares travel distances in a compact city with those in a sprawled one for the same population.

questions.stem: What travel outcome is most likely in the compact city?

options.text: No change in travel behaviour at all.
Longer trips because destinations are clustered.
Shorter average trip lengths and lower car use.
Higher car use due to congestion alone.

questions.explanation: Compactness shortens trips and lowers car use; longer trips or no change are wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Food desert and the access metric
questions.stem: Explain why measuring only distance to a supermarket can misclassify a food desert.

answer.exemplar: Distance alone ignores income and transport access, so an area may have a nearby shop yet residents still cannot afford or reach it.

questions.explanation: Income and transport also matter; distance alone misses affordability and access.
questions.hint: Add income and transport to distance.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Round trip to the nearest food shop
questions.stem: A low-income resident faces a 6 km round trip to food; what barrier is primary?

options.text: Distance never affects low-income shoppers.
The barrier is only about food price.
No barrier exists if the shop is open late.
Time and transport cost dominate the barrier.

questions.explanation: Time and transport cost dominate; price-only or denying distance is wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Use of a park at different distances
questions.learningObjective: Explain distance decay in park use
questions.stem: Explain why park use declines as distance from home increases.

answer.exemplar: Walking time and effort rise with distance, so fewer residents visit; this distance decay shapes how parks should be distributed.

questions.explanation: Rising time and effort reduce visits; omitting the effort factor is incomplete.
